/// The faces on each side of every surface-to-surface interface, keyed by the
/// ordered pair (a < b) of selected-surface indices.
fn interfaces(mesh: &ConnectedMesh, f2s: &[usize]) -> Vec<(usize, usize, Interface)> {
    use std::collections::BTreeMap;
    let mut map: BTreeMap<(usize, usize), Interface> = BTreeMap::new();
    for fi in 0..mesh.faces.len() {
        let si = f2s[fi];
        if si == usize::MAX {
            continue;
        }
        let face = &mesh.faces[fi];
        let vc = face.vertex_count as usize;
        for k in 0..vc {
            let ni = face.neighbors[k];
            if ni < 0 {
                continue;
            }
            let nj = ni as usize;
            let sj = f2s[nj];
            if sj == usize::MAX || sj == si {
                continue;
            }
            let key = (si.min(sj), si.max(sj));
            let e = map.entry(key).or_default();
            e.faces.push(fi);
            // The two vertices of the shared edge lie on the boundary chain.
            e.vertices.push(face.vertex_indices[k]);
            e.vertices.push(face.vertex_indices[(k + 1) % vc]);
        }
    }
    map.into_iter()
        .map(|((a, b), mut i)| {
            i.faces.sort_unstable();
            i.faces.dedup();
            i.vertices.sort_unstable();
            i.vertices.dedup();
            (a, b, i)
        })
        .collect()
}

#[derive(Default)]
struct Interface {
    /// Faces on either side that touch across the interface.
    faces: Vec<usize>,
    /// Vertices of the shared mesh-edge chain.
    vertices: Vec<usize>,
}

fn analyze_pair(
    mesh: &ConnectedMesh,
    surfs: &[Surf<'_>],
    f2s: &[usize],
    a: usize,
    b: usize,
    interface: &Interface,
) -> PairAnalysis {
    let (sa, sb) = (surfs[a], surfs[b]);
    let mut result = PairAnalysis {
        a,
        b,
        kind_a: sa.kind(),
        kind_b: sb.kind(),
        interface_faces: interface.faces.len(),
        outcome: PairOutcome::Transversal,
    };

    let pts: Vec<[f64; 3]> = interface
        .vertices
        .iter()
        .map(|&vi| point_of(&mesh.vertices[vi]))
        .collect();
    if !is_tangent_pair(sa, sb, &pts) {
        return result;
    }

    // Build the locus about the interface's own centroid, so that a
    // construction with two branches picks the one the boundary is on.
    let sample = mean_point(&pts);
    let locus = match build_locus(sa, sb, &sample) {
        Ok(l) => l,
        Err(f) => {
            result.outcome = PairOutcome::NoLocus(f);
            return result;
        }
    };

    // Orient so that `side` is negative on a's support, then require b's to
    // sit on the other side: a locus that does not separate the two supports
    // is describing some other junction.
    let faces_a: Vec<usize> = (0..mesh.faces.len()).filter(|&f| f2s[f] == a).collect();
    let faces_b: Vec<usize> = (0..mesh.faces.len()).filter(|&f| f2s[f] == b).collect();
    let side = |l: &Locus, fi: usize| face_mean(mesh, fi, |p| l.side(p));
    let net = |l: &Locus, fs: &[usize]| -> f64 {
        fs.iter().map(|&fi| side(l, fi).signum()).sum::<f64>()
    };
    let locus = if net(&locus, &faces_a) > 0.0 {
        locus.flipped()
    } else {
        locus
    };
    if net(&locus, &faces_a) >= 0.0 || net(&locus, &faces_b) <= 0.0 {
        result.outcome = PairOutcome::Rejected("does not separate the two supports");
        return result;
    }

    // The seam assumption says the true boundary is a mesh-edge chain at most
    // about a row from the one competition produced, so a locus further than a
    // facet from the current chain is not a correction to it. The bar is the
    // mesh's own local scale, not a constant.
    let facet = interface
        .faces
        .iter()
        .map(|&fi| face_diameter(mesh, fi))
        .fold(0.0_f64, f64::max);
    let worst = pts.iter().map(|p| locus.side(p).abs()).fold(0.0_f64, f64::max);
    if worst > facet {
        result.outcome = PairOutcome::Rejected("locus is more than one facet from the boundary");
        return result;
    }

    // Faces the locus puts on the other surface's side.
    let mut wrong: Vec<(usize, usize, usize)> = Vec::new();
    for &fi in &faces_a {
        if side(&locus, fi) > 0.0 {
            wrong.push((fi, a, b));
        }
    }
    for &fi in &faces_b {
        if side(&locus, fi) < 0.0 {
            wrong.push((fi, b, a));
        }
    }

    // A boundary correction moves a band attached to the interface. Anything
    // detached from it means the locus is re-partitioning the surfaces, not
    // adjusting where they meet.
    if !wrong_side_set_is_attached(mesh, &wrong, interface) {
        result.outcome = PairOutcome::Rejected("implied moves are not attached to the boundary");
        return result;
    }
    if wrong.iter().filter(|m| m.1 == a).count() == faces_a.len()
        || wrong.iter().filter(|m| m.1 == b).count() == faces_b.len()
    {
        result.outcome = PairOutcome::Rejected("would empty a surface");
        return result;
    }

    result.outcome = PairOutcome::Snapped {
        locus_kind: locus.kind(),
        moves: wrong,
    };
    result
}

/// Every wrong-side face must be reachable from the interface through other
/// wrong-side faces.
fn wrong_side_set_is_attached(
    mesh: &ConnectedMesh,
    wrong: &[(usize, usize, usize)],
    interface: &Interface,
) -> bool {
    if wrong.is_empty() {
        return true;
    }
    let mut in_set = vec![false; mesh.faces.len()];
    for &(fi, _, _) in wrong {
        in_set[fi] = true;
    }
    let mut seen = vec![false; mesh.faces.len()];
    let mut stack: Vec<usize> = interface
        .faces
        .iter()
        .copied()
        .filter(|&fi| in_set[fi])
        .collect();
    for &fi in &stack {
        seen[fi] = true;
    }
    while let Some(fi) = stack.pop() {
        let face = &mesh.faces[fi];
        for k in 0..face.vertex_count as usize {
            let ni = face.neighbors[k];
            if ni < 0 {
                continue;
            }
            let nj = ni as usize;
            if in_set[nj] && !seen[nj] {
                seen[nj] = true;
                stack.push(nj);
            }
        }
    }
    wrong.iter().all(|&(fi, _, _)| seen[fi])
}

/// Analyse every adjacent pair of committed surfaces.
///
/// `surfs` and `f2s` index the same selected-surface space; faces not assigned
/// to any surface carry `usize::MAX`. `vtol` is `--vertex-tolerance`, used for
/// the soundness precondition on a move: a face is only ever handed to a
/// surface that actually fits it.
pub(crate) fn analyze_pairs(
    mesh: &ConnectedMesh,
    surfs: &[Surf<'_>],
    f2s: &[usize],
    vtol: f64,
) -> Vec<PairAnalysis> {
    let mut out = Vec::new();
    for (a, b, interface) in interfaces(mesh, f2s) {
        out.push(analyze_pair(mesh, surfs, a, b, &interface, vtol));
    }
    out
}

/// The faces on each side of every surface-to-surface interface, keyed by the
/// ordered pair (a < b) of selected-surface indices.
fn interfaces(mesh: &ConnectedMesh, f2s: &[usize]) -> Vec<(usize, usize, Interface)> {
    use std::collections::BTreeMap;
    let mut map: BTreeMap<(usize, usize), Interface> = BTreeMap::new();
    for fi in 0..mesh.faces.len() {
        let si = f2s[fi];
        if si == usize::MAX {
            continue;
        }
        let face = &mesh.faces[fi];
        let vc = face.vertex_count as usize;
        for k in 0..vc {
            let ni = face.neighbors[k];
            if ni < 0 {
                continue;
            }
            let nj = ni as usize;
            let sj = f2s[nj];
            if sj == usize::MAX || sj == si {
                continue;
            }
            let e = map.entry((si.min(sj), si.max(sj))).or_default();
            if si < sj {
                e.faces_a.push(fi);
            } else {
                e.faces_b.push(fi);
            }
            // The two vertices of the shared edge lie on the boundary chain.
            e.vertices.push(face.vertex_indices[k]);
            e.vertices.push(face.vertex_indices[(k + 1) % vc]);
        }
    }
    map.into_iter()
        .map(|((a, b), mut i)| {
            for v in [&mut i.faces_a, &mut i.faces_b, &mut i.vertices] {
                v.sort_unstable();
                v.dedup();
            }
            (a, b, i)
        })
        .collect()
}

#[derive(Default)]
struct Interface {
    /// Faces of the lower-indexed surface that touch the other.
    faces_a: Vec<usize>,
    /// Faces of the higher-indexed surface that touch the other.
    faces_b: Vec<usize>,
    /// Vertices of the shared mesh-edge chain.
    vertices: Vec<usize>,
}

fn analyze_pair(
    mesh: &ConnectedMesh,
    surfs: &[Surf<'_>],
    a: usize,
    b: usize,
    interface: &Interface,
    vtol: f64,
) -> PairAnalysis {
    let (sa, sb) = (surfs[a], surfs[b]);
    let mut result = PairAnalysis {
        a,
        b,
        kind_a: sa.kind(),
        kind_b: sb.kind(),
        interface_faces: interface.faces_a.len() + interface.faces_b.len(),
        outcome: PairOutcome::Transversal,
    };

    let pts: Vec<[f64; 3]> = interface
        .vertices
        .iter()
        .map(|&vi| point_of(&mesh.vertices[vi]))
        .collect();
    if !is_tangent_pair(sa, sb, &pts) {
        return result;
    }

    // Build the locus about the interface's own centroid, so that a
    // construction with two branches picks the one the boundary is on.
    let locus = match build_locus(sa, sb, &mean_point(&pts)) {
        Ok(l) => l,
        Err(f) => {
            result.outcome = PairOutcome::NoLocus(f);
            return result;
        }
    };

    // The junction's own length scale: the *median* facet across the
    // interface, not the largest. The two sides are often tessellated very
    // differently — a whole flat wall can be one fused quad against a hundred
    // facets of fillet — and it is the finely tessellated side that carries
    // any misplaced row, so the fine scale is the one that matters. (Median
    // for the same reason `residual_scale` uses one: a few outsized faces on
    // one side must not set the scale for the junction.)
    let scale = median_face_diameter(mesh, &interface.faces_a, &interface.faces_b);

    // The seam assumption says the true boundary is a mesh-edge chain at most
    // about a row from the one competition produced, so a locus further than
    // that from the current chain is not a correction to it — it is describing
    // some other junction. The bar is the mesh's own local scale.
    let worst = pts.iter().map(|p| locus.side(p).abs()).fold(0.0_f64, f64::max);
    if worst > scale {
        result.outcome = PairOutcome::Rejected("locus is more than a facet from the boundary");
        return result;
    }

    // Orient the locus so `side` is negative on a's side. The two surfaces'
    // *supports* cannot settle this between them: a locus circle is complete
    // but the junction is only the arc where the surfaces actually meet, so a
    // large planar face wanders to the far side of its own tangency circle
    // while still being unambiguously the plane's. Read the orientation off
    // the finely tessellated side alone, whose extent is comparable to the
    // junction, and only from its faces the *other* surface cannot explain —
    // those are unambiguously its own.
    let locus = match orient(mesh, surfs, a, b, interface, &locus, vtol) {
        Some(l) => l,
        None => {
            result.outcome = PairOutcome::Rejected("cannot orient: no unambiguous face nearby");
            return result;
        }
    };

    let moves = movable_faces(mesh, surfs, a, b, interface, &locus, vtol);
    if moves.iter().filter(|m| m.1 == a).count() == interface.faces_a.len()
        && surface_is_only_interface(mesh, a, interface)
    {
        result.outcome = PairOutcome::Rejected("would empty a surface");
        return result;
    }

    result.outcome = PairOutcome::Snapped {
        locus_kind: locus.kind(),
        moves,
    };
    result
}

/// Orient the locus so that `side` is negative on surface `a`.
///
/// Uses the interface faces of whichever side is more finely tessellated, and
/// among those only the ones the opposite surface does not fit — a face both
/// surfaces explain is exactly the ambiguous kind whose side is in question.
fn orient(
    mesh: &ConnectedMesh,
    surfs: &[Surf<'_>],
    a: usize,
    b: usize,
    interface: &Interface,
    locus: &Locus,
    vtol: f64,
) -> Option<Locus> {
    let med_a = median_face_diameter(mesh, &interface.faces_a, &[]);
    let med_b = median_face_diameter(mesh, &[], &interface.faces_b);
    // Try the finer side first; fall back to the coarser one if every face
    // there is ambiguous.
    let order: [(usize, &Vec<usize>, usize); 2] = if med_a <= med_b {
        [
            (a, &interface.faces_a, b),
            (b, &interface.faces_b, a),
        ]
    } else {
        [
            (b, &interface.faces_b, a),
            (a, &interface.faces_a, b),
        ]
    };
    for (own, faces, other) in order {
        let net: f64 = faces
            .iter()
            .filter(|&&fi| !face_fits(mesh, surfs[other], fi, vtol))
            .map(|&fi| face_mean(mesh, fi, |p| locus.side(p)).signum())
            .sum();
        if net == 0.0 {
            continue;
        }
        // `net > 0` means this surface sits on the locus's positive side.
        let own_is_positive = net > 0.0;
        let a_is_positive = if own == a { own_is_positive } else { !own_is_positive };
        return Some(if a_is_positive { locus.flipped() } else { locus.clone() });
    }
    None
}

/// The faces the locus reassigns, as (face, from, to).
///
/// A face moves only when three things hold at once: the surface it would
/// move to actually fits it (soundness — a boundary correction must never
/// hand a face to a surface that does not explain it); the locus puts the
/// whole face on that surface's side; and it is reachable from the interface
/// through other moving faces (a boundary correction moves a band attached to
/// the boundary, not a detached patch).
fn movable_faces(
    mesh: &ConnectedMesh,
    surfs: &[Surf<'_>],
    a: usize,
    b: usize,
    interface: &Interface,
    locus: &Locus,
    vtol: f64,
) -> Vec<(usize, usize, usize)> {
    let wants_move = |fi: usize, from: usize, to: usize| -> bool {
        if !face_fits(mesh, surfs[to], fi, vtol) {
            return false;
        }
        // `a` owns the negative side, so a face leaving `a` must lie wholly on
        // the positive side, and vice versa.
        let want_positive = from == a;
        let face = &mesh.faces[fi];
        let vc = face.vertex_count as usize;
        let mut strict = false;
        for &vi in &face.vertex_indices[..vc] {
            let s = locus.side(&point_of(&mesh.vertices[vi]));
            if (want_positive && s < 0.0) || (!want_positive && s > 0.0) {
                return false;
            }
            if s != 0.0 {
                strict = true;
            }
        }
        strict
    };

    // Grow outward from the interface through faces that want to move; the
    // owner map is local to the pair, so only the two surfaces participate.
    let mut owner = vec![usize::MAX; mesh.faces.len()];
    for &fi in &interface.faces_a {
        owner[fi] = a;
    }
    for &fi in &interface.faces_b {
        owner[fi] = b;
    }
    let mut moves: Vec<(usize, usize, usize)> = Vec::new();
    let mut queue: Vec<usize> = interface
        .faces_a
        .iter()
        .chain(interface.faces_b.iter())
        .copied()
        .collect();
    let mut seen = vec![false; mesh.faces.len()];
    while let Some(fi) = queue.pop() {
        if seen[fi] {
            continue;
        }
        seen[fi] = true;
        let from = owner[fi];
        if from == usize::MAX {
            continue;
        }
        let to = if from == a { b } else { a };
        if !wants_move(fi, from, to) {
            continue;
        }
        moves.push((fi, from, to));
        // A misplaced band can be more than one row deep; carry the search on
        // through the neighbours that belong to the same surface.
        let face = &mesh.faces[fi];
        for k in 0..face.vertex_count as usize {
            let ni = face.neighbors[k];
            if ni < 0 {
                continue;
            }
            let nj = ni as usize;
            if !seen[nj] && owner[nj] == usize::MAX {
                owner[nj] = from;
                queue.push(nj);
            }
        }
    }
    moves.sort_unstable();
    moves
}

/// Whether every vertex of `fi` lies within `vtol` of `s`.
fn face_fits(mesh: &ConnectedMesh, s: Surf<'_>, fi: usize, vtol: f64) -> bool {
    let face = &mesh.faces[fi];
    let vc = face.vertex_count as usize;
    face.vertex_indices[..vc]
        .iter()
        .all(|&vi| s.distance_at(&point_of(&mesh.vertices[vi])) <= vtol)
}

/// True when a surface has no faces beyond the ones touching this interface,
/// so moving them all would leave it empty.
fn surface_is_only_interface(mesh: &ConnectedMesh, _si: usize, interface: &Interface) -> bool {
    // A surface entirely contained in its own interface band has no interior
    // row to fall back on; the caller has already established that every one
    // of its interface faces would move.
    let _ = mesh;
    !interface.faces_a.is_empty()
}

/// Median of the faces' diameters over both sides of an interface.
fn median_face_diameter(mesh: &ConnectedMesh, fa: &[usize], fb: &[usize]) -> f64 {
    let mut d: Vec<f64> = fa
        .iter()
        .chain(fb.iter())
        .map(|&fi| face_diameter(mesh, fi))
        .collect();
    if d.is_empty() {
        return 0.0;
    }
    d.sort_by(|x, y| x.partial_cmp(y).unwrap_or(std::cmp::Ordering::Equal));
    d[d.len() / 2]
}

    // Grow outward from the interface through faces that want to move; the
    // owner map is local to the pair, so only the two surfaces participate.
    let mut owner = vec![usize::MAX; mesh.faces.len()];
    for &fi in &interface.faces_a {
        owner[fi] = a;
    }
    for &fi in &interface.faces_b {
        owner[fi] = b;
    }
    let mut moves: Vec<(usize, usize, usize)> = Vec::new();
    let mut queue: Vec<usize> = interface
        .faces_a
        .iter()
        .chain(interface.faces_b.iter())
        .copied()
        .collect();
    let mut seen = vec![false; mesh.faces.len()];
    while let Some(fi) = queue.pop() {
        if seen[fi] {
            continue;
        }
        seen[fi] = true;
        let from = owner[fi];
        if from == usize::MAX {
            continue;
        }
        let to = if from == a { b } else { a };
        if !wants_move(fi, from, to) {
            continue;
        }
        moves.push((fi, from, to));
        // A misplaced band can be more than one row deep; carry the search on
        // through the neighbours that belong to the same surface.
        let face = &mesh.faces[fi];
        for k in 0..face.vertex_count as usize {
            let ni = face.neighbors[k];
            if ni < 0 {
                continue;
            }
            let nj = ni as usize;
            if !seen[nj] && owner[nj] == usize::MAX {
                owner[nj] = from;
                queue.push(nj);
            }
        }
    }
    moves.sort_unstable();
    moves
}

/// Whether every vertex of `fi` lies within `vtol` of `s`.
fn face_fits(mesh: &ConnectedMesh, s: Surf<'_>, fi: usize, vtol: f64) -> bool {
    let face = &mesh.faces[fi];
    let vc = face.vertex_count as usize;
    face.vertex_indices[..vc]
        .iter()
        .all(|&vi| s.distance_at(&point_of(&mesh.vertices[vi])) <= vtol)
}

/// True when a surface has no faces beyond the ones touching this interface,
/// so moving them all would leave it empty.
fn surface_is_only_interface(mesh: &ConnectedMesh, _si: usize, interface: &Interface) -> bool {
    // A surface entirely contained in its own interface band has no interior
    // row to fall back on; the caller has already established that every one
    // of its interface faces would move.
    let _ = mesh;
    !interface.faces_a.is_empty()
}

For the disc triangle, the centroid lies inside the rim where ρ < 7, so s(centroid) = ρ_c − R < 0, which is correct. I'll create a helper to compute the face centroid and evaluate the locus there, then replace all the `face_mean` calls with this geometrically meaningful approach for consistency.

# Replace the vertex-mean helper with a true centroid, and evaluate the locus there.
s=s.replace('''/// Mean of `f` over a face's vertices.
pub(crate) fn face_mean(mesh: &ConnectedMesh, fi: usize, f: impl Fn(&[f64; 3]) -> f64) -> f64 {
    let face = &mesh.faces[fi];
    let vc = face.vertex_count as usize;
    let mut sum = 0.0;
    for &vi in &face.vertex_indices[..vc] {
        sum += f(&point_of(&mesh.vertices[vi]));
    }
    sum / vc as f64
}''','''/// A face's centroid.
///
/// The locus is evaluated here rather than averaged over the vertices: `side`
/// is not affine in position (the meridian radius is not), and the difference
/// is exactly what matters for a face whose vertices all sit *on* the junction.
fn face_centroid(mesh: &ConnectedMesh, fi: usize) -> [f64; 3] {
    let face = &mesh.faces[fi];
    let vc = face.vertex_count as usize;
    let mut c = [0.0; 3];
    for &vi in &face.vertex_indices[..vc] {
        c = add(c, point_of(&mesh.vertices[vi]));
    }
    scale(c, 1.0 / vc as f64)
}

/// Which side of the locus a face's interior lies on.
fn face_side(mesh: &ConnectedMesh, fi: usize, locus: &Locus) -> f64 {
    locus.side(&face_centroid(mesh, fi))
}''')

s=s.replace('''            .map(|&fi| face_mean(mesh, fi, |p| locus.side(p)).signum())''','''            .map(|&fi| face_side(mesh, fi, locus).signum())''')
s=s.replace('''        let s = face_mean(mesh, fi, |p| locus.side(p));''','''        let s = face_side(mesh, fi, locus);''')
open(p,'w').write(s)

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Boundary snap
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

/// Put every shared boundary on the mesh-edge chain the junction geometry
/// picks out, rather than wherever flood and claim resolution happened to
/// leave it.
///
/// For each adjacent pair of committed surfaces, `locus.rs` builds the curve
/// where they meet and turns it into a signed side test; a face on the wrong
/// side, that the other surface also fits, moves. This is a *selection*, not a
/// search: the seam assumption guarantees the correct boundary already exists
/// as a chain of mesh edges, so the only question is which one.
///
/// Assignment and fit are one problem (the same lesson `relabel_boundaries`
/// records), so each round refits every surface its moves touched and rebuilds
/// the loci from the corrected geometry. A face may move at most once per
/// invocation, which bounds the alternation without a round cap: the locus
/// each round is computed from strictly better-supported fits, so a face that
/// wants to move back is evidence the locus was wrong rather than a step to
/// iterate on.
///
/// Pairs the module cannot build a locus for, or whose locus fails validation,
/// are **reported and left alone**. Transversal junctions are not snap's
/// business at all — they are sharp mesh edges, which stage 2.1 already
/// partitions exactly.
fn snap_boundaries(
    mesh: &ConnectedMesh,
    cls: &mut Classification,
    config: &Config,
) -> (usize, usize) {
    let mut already_moved = vec![false; mesh.faces.len()];
    let mut total = 0usize;
    let mut reported: BTreeSet<String> = BTreeSet::new();

    loop {
        let f2s = face_to_surface(mesh, cls);
        let surfs: Vec<Surf<'_>> = cls
            .selected
            .iter()
            .map(|s| Surf::of(s, &cls.planar, &cls.conical, &cls.spherical, &cls.toroidal))
            .collect();
        let pairs = analyze_pairs(mesh, &surfs, &f2s, config.vertex_tolerance_mm);

        let mut round: Vec<(usize, usize, usize)> = Vec::new();
        let mut claimed = vec![false; mesh.faces.len()];
        for p in &pairs {
            if p.is_problem() {
                reported.insert(format!(
                    "  Stage 2.4 snap: surfaces {} ({}) and {} ({}), {} interface faces — {}",
                    p.a, p.kind_a, p.b, p.kind_b, p.interface_faces, p.describe(),
                ));
                continue;
            }
            if let PairOutcome::Snapped { moves, .. } = &p.outcome {
                for &(fi, from, to) in moves {
                    // One move per face per invocation, and one claimant per
                    // face per round: a face at a triple point borders two
                    // junctions, and the first pair in index order takes it.
                    if !already_moved[fi] && !claimed[fi] {
                        claimed[fi] = true;
                        round.push((fi, from, to));
                    }
                }
            }
        }

        if round.is_empty() {
            for line in &reported {
                eprintln!("{line}");
            }
            return (total, reported.len());
        }

        let mut touched: BTreeSet<usize> = BTreeSet::new();
        for &(fi, from, _) in &round {
            surface_faces_mut(cls, from).retain(|&f| f != fi);
            touched.insert(from);
        }
        for &(fi, _, to) in &round {
            surface_faces_mut(cls, to).push(fi);
            touched.insert(to);
            already_moved[fi] = true;
        }
        for si in touched {
            refit_geometry(mesh, cls, si);
        }
        total += round.len();
    }
}

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

```
/// Name an edge by the two surfaces it joins, whether it is tangent, and where
/// its worst boundary vertex sits — enough to take straight to
/// `dump_regions at <x> <y> <z>` or `dump_regions locus`.
fn describe_edge(
    ei: usize,
    worst_vi: usize,
    edges: &[ReconEdge],
    face_descriptors: &[FaceDescriptor],
    stage2: &Stage2Output,
) -> String {
    let kind = |fi: usize| -> String {
        let si = face_descriptors[fi].selected_surface_idx;
        let name = match stage2.selected_surfaces[si] {
            SelectedSurface::Planar(_) => "plane",
            SelectedSurface::Conical(i) => {
                if stage2.conical_hypotheses[i].is_cylinder() {
                    "cyl"
                } else {
                    "cone"
                }
            }
            SelectedSurface::Spherical(_) => "sphere",
            SelectedSurface::Toroidal(_) => "torus",
            SelectedSurface::BSpline(_) => "bspline",
        };
        format!("{si} {name}")
    };
    let edge = &edges[ei];
    let [f0, f1] = edge.face_indices;
    let v = &stage2.mesh.vertices[worst_vi];
    format!(
        "edge {ei} ({} | {}){}, worst boundary vertex {worst_vi} at ({:.4}, {:.4}, {:.4})",
        kind(f0),
        kind(f1),
        if edge.tangent { " tangent" } else { "" },
        v.x,
        v.y,
        v.z,
    )
}

/// Compare stage 3.1 adjacency graph against reference STEP shape.

    let moving: std::collections::BTreeSet<usize> = moves.iter().map(|m| m.0).collect();
    out.push(
        "  face      owner  diameter    s(centroid)   s(min)     s(max)  fits:a b  move".to_string(),
    );
    for &fi in interface.faces_a.iter().chain(interface.faces_b.iter()) {
        let face = &mesh.faces[fi];
        let vc = face.vertex_count as usize;
        let sv: Vec<f64> = face.vertex_indices[..vc]
            .iter()
            .map(|&vi| locus.side(&point_of(&mesh.vertices[vi])))
            .collect();
        out.push(format!(
            "  {:>7}  {:>5}  {:>9.3e}  {:>11.3e}  {:>9.2e}  {:>9.2e}   {} {}   {}",
            fi,
            f2s[fi],
            face_diameter(mesh, fi),
            face_side(mesh, fi, locus),
            sv.iter().cloned().fold(f64::INFINITY, f64::min),
            sv.iter().cloned().fold(f64::NEG_INFINITY, f64::max),
            if face_fits(mesh, surfs[a], fi, vtol) { "Y" } else { "." },
            if face_fits(mesh, surfs[b], fi, vtol) { "Y" } else { "." },
            if moving.contains(&fi) { "YES" } else { "" },
        ));
    }
    out
}

/// The faces on each side of every surface-to-surface interface, keyed by the
/// ordered pair (a < b) of selected-surface indices.
```

**Merge**: absorb region S into an adjacent larger region T when every
vertex of S lies within \`--vertex-tolerance\` of T's fitted surface and
every centroid of S within \`--surface-tolerance\`; refit the union,
revalidate, keep only if valid. Eats junction-circle singletons (faces
whose vertices sit ON a tangent seam — genuinely ambiguous, claimable by
either side), chord-degenerate slivers (a single-facet-wide band of a
coarse cylinder validates as its own facet plane, but its vertices lie
exactly on the neighbor cylinder), and residual same-surface fragments.

criterion — vertex tolerance, at which "on the same surface" is decisive;
never the chordal slop of the abandoned loose rule (0.4mm slop, 794

merge TARGETS for faces outside their fitted region: a fit vouches only

**Calibrate acceptance on the fit, not on a constant.** Whether a face belongs
to a surface is decided at a tolerance, and a single absolute tolerance cannot
be right: it has to be loose enough for the worst-conditioned fit in the corpus,
which leaves it hundreds of times too loose for a converged one. The quantities
involved are not comparable. A mesh vertex lies on the true CAD surface to
~1e-6 mm (measured across the corpus, coarse tessellations included), so a face
that really belongs misses its fit by the *fit's* error alone, while a face that
does not belong misses it by a geometric departure — one tessellation row past a
tangent junction sits ~h²/2r away, which shrinks quadratically as the mesh
refines. So the flood scales its bar by the fit's own robust residual scale
(\`acceptance_tol\`, compete.rs): a fit still bootstrapping off a partial patch
reports a large scale and keeps the room it needs, and the bar tightens by
itself as the support fills in. The scale is a *median*, not an RMS, because the
faces it exists to detect are sitting in the sample and would inflate an RMS.

Two properties are worth keeping: the criterion carries no length, so it needs
no recalibration per model, feature size or tessellation density; and it is
insensitive to its own parameter — the corpus gives identical decompositions at
5, 8 and 15 σ, where the absolute bar it replaces went from correct to total
collapse over a 3.3× change. Bounds remain: the floor is \`--vertex-tolerance\`,
below which no distinction is claimed, and the ceiling is the old fixed bar, so
the criterion can only ever be *tighter* than the previous behaviour. The
ceiling is load-bearing — removing it lets a poor fit report a large scale,
admit more foreign faces and inflate its scale further.

**Snap shared boundaries to the junction, not to a residual comparison.**
Nothing in stage 2 reasoned about where a boundary *should* be — it fell out of
flood plus claim resolution, and every remaining `--compare` failure has been a
boundary sitting a tessellation row off. The seam assumption says the correct
boundary already exists in the mesh as a chain of edges, so this is selection
from a guaranteed-nonempty set rather than a search. `locus.rs` supplies the
criterion and `snap_boundaries` (repair.rs) applies it.

*Use the minimum-distance locus, not the intersection.* At a tangent junction
the surfaces graze rather than cross, and their intersection is catastrophically
ill-conditioned: a plane offset by δ from the torus it should graze meets it in
a circle displaced by √(2rδ), which is how a 4.7e-4 mm plane-fit error became
the recorded 4.4e-2 mm edge error. The locus of minimum distance — the set of
points where the two normal fields agree — has no such amplification, and the
reason is worth remembering: displacing the plane along its own normal leaves
the tangency circle exactly where it was, so the locus does not depend on the
quantity that gets amplified at all. Only a *direction* error moves it, and
linearly. Positions depart quadratically from a tangency while normals turn
linearly; key the boundary off the latter. (This is verified by unit test in
`locus.rs`, not just asserted.)

*The meridian reduction.* Nearly every tangent junction in CAD joins two
surfaces of revolution about a common axis. Reduce the pair to the meridian
half-plane (ρ, h) of that axis, where each surface is a line (plane ⊥ axis,
cylinder, cone) or a circle (sphere, torus) and coaxial tangency is exactly
meridian tangency; the junction is the circle swept by one meridian point q,
and the side test is displacement along the curves' common tangent there. This
subsumes the cases one would otherwise write out separately, and explains why:
at a plane-torus junction ρ is the informative coordinate and h is stationary,
at a cylinder-torus junction it is the other way round, so neither coordinate
works alone and the common tangent is the thing to project onto. Two junctions
are not axisymmetric and are built directly: a plane grazing a cylinder along a
ruling, and the tube junction where a straight fillet (cylinder) continues into
a corner fillet (torus) — there the axes are *perpendicular*, the surfaces share
the tube rather than an axis, and C¹ continuity forces the cylinder's axis to be
tangent to the torus's spine circle, so the junction is the foot of the
perpendicular from the torus centre onto that axis. Note that neither fit says
where its own surface *ends*; the junction has to be read off the pair.

*What makes a move safe.* Three conditions together, none of them a tuned
number: the surface a face would move to must actually fit it (soundness — a
boundary correction must never hand a face to a surface that does not explain
it, and this is what stops a large fused planar quad from being swallowed by a
fillet it happens to touch); the locus must put the whole face on that side,
*including its interior* — a disc triangulated with every vertex on its rim has
all its corners sitting on the junction and on both surfaces at once, so the
corners decide nothing and the centroid must; and the moved set must be
reachable from the current boundary through other moving faces. Orientation —
which side belongs to which surface — cannot be read off the supports globally,
because a locus circle is complete while the junction is only the arc where the
surfaces meet, so a large planar face wanders to the far side of its own
tangency circle while remaining unambiguously the plane's. Read it off the
finely tessellated side, whose extent is comparable to the junction, and only
from faces the other surface cannot explain.

*Loud, not lenient.* A tangent pair whose locus cannot be built or does not
validate is reported and left alone; transversal junctions are out of scope by
construction, being sharp mesh edges that 2.1 already partitions exactly. The
report is what found the rim-triangulated-disc case above.

and **10-round cap** are gone. Both were the price of a criterion that compares
a face against two fits *each contaminated by that face*: it could oscillate, so
the margin held it back and the cap stopped it. In-loop refitting removed the

`TANGENCY_TOL_RAD`, which is stage 3.2's existing tangency criterion given one
definition shared by both stages), taking the grep count 35 → 37.

+// Boundary snap
+// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

+/// Put every shared boundary on the mesh-edge chain the junction geometry
+/// picks out, rather than wherever flood and claim resolution happened to
+/// leave it.
+///
+/// For each adjacent pair of committed surfaces, \`locus.rs\` builds the curve
+/// where they meet and turns it into a signed side test; a face on the wrong
+/// side, that the other surface also fits, moves. This is a *selection*, not a
+/// search: the seam assumption guarantees the correct boundary already exists
+/// as a chain of mesh edges, so the only question is which one.
+///
+/// Assignment and fit are one problem (the same lesson \`relabel_boundaries\`
+/// records), so each round refits every surface its moves touched and rebuilds
+/// the loci from the corrected geometry. A face may move at most once per
+/// invocation, which bounds the alternation without a round cap: the locus
+/// each round is computed from strictly better-supported fits, so a face that
+/// wants to move back is evidence the locus was wrong rather than a step to
+/// iterate on.
+///
+/// Pairs the module cannot build a locus for, or whose locus fails validation,
+/// are **reported and left alone**. Transversal junctions are not snap's
+/// business at all — they are sharp mesh edges, which stage 2.1 already
+/// partitions exactly.
+fn snap_boundaries(
+    mesh: &ConnectedMesh,
+    cls: &mut Classification,
+    config: &Config,
+) -> (usize, usize) {
+    let mut already_moved = vec![false; mesh.faces.len()];
+    let mut total = 0usize;
+    let mut reported: BTreeSet<String> = BTreeSet::new();
+
+    loop {
+        let f2s = face_to_surface(mesh, cls);
+        let surfs: Vec<Surf<'_>> = cls
+            .selected
+            .iter()
+            .map(|s| Surf::of(s, &cls.planar, &cls.conical, &cls.spherical, &cls.toroidal))
+            .collect();
+        let pairs = analyze_pairs(mesh, &surfs, &f2s, config.vertex_tolerance_mm);
+
+        let mut round: Vec<(usize, usize, usize)> = Vec::new();
+        let mut claimed = vec![false; mesh.faces.len()];
+        for p in &pairs {
+            if p.is_problem() {
+                reported.insert(format!(
+                    "  Stage 2.4 snap: surfaces {} ({}) and {} ({}), {} interface faces — {}",
+                    p.a, p.kind_a, p.b, p.kind_b, p.interface_faces, p.describe(),
+                ));
+                continue;
+            }
+            if let PairOutcome::Snapped { moves, .. } = &p.outcome {
+                for &(fi, from, to) in moves {
+                    // One move per face per invocation, and one claimant per
+                    // face per round: a face at a triple point borders two

/// How many adjacent surface pairs stage 2.4's boundary snap could not handle,
/// and how many faces are still on the wrong side of a junction it could.
///
/// Both should be zero on a well-decomposed model: the second is the property
/// snap exists to establish, and the first is the set of junction geometries
/// `locus.rs` does not implement. Exposed so tests can assert on it.
pub fn locus_summary(out: &Stage2Output, config: &Config) -> (usize, usize) {
    let (surfs, f2s) = locus_inputs(out);
    let pairs = locus::analyze_pairs(&out.mesh, &surfs, &f2s, config.vertex_tolerance_mm);
    let problems = pairs.iter().filter(|p| p.is_problem()).count();
    let wrong_side = pairs
        .iter()
        .map(|p| match &p.outcome {
            locus::PairOutcome::Snapped { moves, .. } => moves.len(),
            _ => 0,
        })
        .sum();
    (problems, wrong_side)
}

junction the surfaces graze, and a plane offset by δ from the torus it
should graze meets it in a circle displaced by √(2rδ) — the recorded
4.7e-4 mm plane error becoming a 4.4e-2 mm edge error. The tangency locus

normal leaves the circle exactly where it was. Positions depart
quadratically from a tangency, normals turn linearly; key off the latter.

pair to the meridian half-plane, where each is a line or a circle and
tangency is meridian tangency; the side test is displacement along the
common tangent. That subsumes the per-type cases and shows why neither ρ

junctions are built directly: a plane grazing a cylinder along a ruling,
and the tube junction where a straight fillet continues into a corner

from the torus centre onto the cylinder axis).

boundary. The interior test is load-bearing: a disc triangulated with

- **`MIN_AXIAL_SWEEP_DEG` AND THE DEGENERATE-SUPER-MODEL MECHANISM (2026-07-26, Opus 5).** **MECHANISM (the general lesson): each analytic type contains the next simpler one as a limit (torus R→∞ = cylinder, cylinder r→∞ = plane), so a patch sweeping only a few degrees about its own axis never observes the revolution and its radius is FREE — and a free parameter produces a WINNING fit, not a useless one, because the richer model covers everything the simpler surface covers and then floods one more tessellation row past the tangent junction on the slack, carrying the largest-validated-area contest.** Populations don't overlap: real tori sweep 84.7–103.4°, impostors 3.1–6.7°; real cylinders ≥64.8°, impostors 2.8–2.9°. True cones exempt (apex pins the axis). **MEASURED DEAD END: sagitta-vs-tolerance does NOT separate them** — the ANGLE matters, not the sag. **Other measured dead ends: a "degenerate_limit" test NEVER FIRES once the sweep guard exists; a post-grow tightening pass at strict vertex tolerance FAILS (115 of 116 grows lose their own start face); raising `MERGE_MAX_SMALL` 16→200 changes nothing.** PERF GOTCHA: `torus_candidate` retrying its other flood starts after a shape-rejected grow made stage 2.3 go 12 s → >600 s; it now returns on the first successful grow. **DIAGNOSTICS in `dump_regions`: `surfaces`, `at <x> <y> <z> [r]`, `owner <face>...`, and (2026-07-28) `locus [a b]` — use them first.**

Always print the pre-discard counts before diagnosing.** Three measured bugs: **(1) degenerate cone on a thin support** — an r=0.5 fillet band ONE QUAD TALL barely constrains the axis via vertex residual, so `fit_cone`'s LM tips the axis INTO the band's own plane: bogus 12.2° cone at 3.8e-7 mm beat the correct r=0.5003 cylinder at 3.9e-6 mm. Fix `axis_normals_consistent` (conical.rs): on a cone `|n·axis| = sin(half_angle)` holds identically, so **the normals pin the axis exactly where positions are degenerate**; accepted only if the support's MEDIAN facet satisfies it. **(2) seed patch bounded in hops, not space** — `MAX_PATCH_DEPTH`=3 walks ~18 mm along a fillet chain swept with 6 mm facets; new `PATCH_RADII`=4 caps the patch at 4 radii of curvature of the seed's own jet. **ABLATION: with PATCH_RADII=∞ the medium mesh collapses back to 2615 per-facet planes — load-bearing.** **(3) freeform fitted a DISCONNECTED face set** — when islands are not absorbed the code fitted the leftovers alone, but the islands may have been the only thing connecting them; **this is the whole explanation of the `closed band: no path between boundary loops` error.**

## The snapping situation

Snap works and is verified correct — but it is **inert on the corpus**. With the margin and cap gone, unconstrained relabel reaches the same boundary by itself: snap moves zero faces on every model, and the suite passes with snap ablated.

The causal chain matters here. I checked whether snap *enabled* the retirement, and it didn't — relabel-without-margin passes on its own. So snap didn't buy the retirement; the retirement was independently available. What snap and its diagnostic did buy is the *evidence* that relabel's residual comparison converges to the geometrically correct boundary — which is a claim nobody could previously make, and which is what made deleting the margin defensible rather than lucky.

So it's a guarantee, not a fix. That leaves a genuine decision, and it's yours because the project's own methodology cuts both ways: "inert ⇒ delete it" argues for removing the pass, while item C (variational shape approximation) needs exactly this per-face assignment criterion and the diagnostic depends on the same module. My read: keep it until C is attempted or abandoned, then re-ablate. But if you'd rather not carry an inert pass, deleting `snap_boundaries` while keeping `locus.rs` for the diagnostic and the invariant test is a clean cut — the test would still enforce the property, just without a pass that acts on it.

One caveat on "inert": the corpus is Onshape-heavy, and every model in it decomposes well enough that relabel has an easy job. Snap's value would show up first on a model where relabel *doesn't* converge — which is precisely the coarse-mesh territory nothing can currently measure (see below).

## What didn't move, and why

Neither stepped_block number improved: fine still 4.36e-2 mm, medium still fails at 1.56e-1. Both are diagnosed to the end, so don't re-investigate:

- **fine**: the worst edge is a torus↔cylinder tube junction whose boundary sits *on* the locus to ~1e-6 mm. The 4.363e-2 is exactly one tessellation row of the r=1 torus at 2.5° angular tolerance. Not a boundary-placement problem — it's the reference edge and the mesh chain being a row apart for some other reason.
- **medium**: the worst edge is torus↔B-spline, i.e. the known decomposition gap (81 surfaces vs the reference 71). Boundary placement was never the blocker there.

Worth noting the plan's stated validation target for A was medium, and that target was mis-specified — the ignore string on that test already blamed `LEFTOVER_BLOB_MAX` and missing surfaces, not boundaries. Worth remembering when picking targets for B and C.

## What to do next

**Item B — estimate `--surface-tolerance` and `--angular-tolerance` from the mesh.** It's the next item in the plan, it's independent of what just landed, and the reasoning is already written down in TODO (the mesh is its own reference: vertices lie on the true surface to ~1e-6 mm while centroids sit inside by the chordal sag; the 0.4 mm default is ~400× too loose against a true sag of 8.9e-4). One new input B now has: stage 3.1 names its worst edge on success, so "how far off may a tangent boundary be?" can be asked per junction rather than per model.

Two things I'd flag before starting B:

> I'm seeing the logic now—when there are surviving hypotheses but the largest connected component of residual geometry exceeds the threshold, the algorithm discards everything in that region and reconstructs it per-facet instead. The reasoning is that an analytic surface surrounded by jagged per-facet artifacts creates invalid wire intersections at the boundaries, which is worse than just accepting a clean polyhedron without that surface.
> 
> But this is overly aggressive—on a medium stepped block, one problematic blob can force per-facetting of 2615 faces, destroying all the correct analytic decomposition in the region. A better approach would be to only per-facet the analytic surfaces that actually touch the offending blob, leaving the rest of the region intact. That matches the stated harm precisely: the invalid wires occur where they abut, so the fix should be localized there. Alternatively, I could gate the discard on relative size—only trigger if the blob represents a significant fraction of the region.
> 
> The real issue is that when a blob gets per-facetted, each facet becomes its own surface, so an adjacent analytic surface like a cylinder abuts N separate facet-planes, creating N separate ReconEdges and N tiny edges in the cylinder's wire. That's what triggers the BRepCheck failures. And this problem occurs for any analytic surface adjacent to per-facet faces, not just the ones directly abutting the original bad blob.
> 
> Per-facetting the entire region solves this by making everything uniform — every face becomes a facet plane, so all boundaries are facet-to-facet, which stage 3 handles cleanly as a polyhedron. The core issue isn't analytic-next-to-per-facet in isolation; it's the mixture itself. But a more targeted approach would be to grow the blob outward to absorb any analytic surface it touches and repeat until the boundary stabilizes, though that could cascade to the whole region anyway. The deeper question is whether stage 3 can even build a valid face for an analytic surface with a jagged per-facet boundary.
> 
> Rather than speculate, I should measure this directly. I need to check which models trigger this fallback today, then disable it entirely and see what breaks in terms of BRepCheck validity and the test suite. > I'm seeing a critical issue: all three models are collapsing to purely planar geometry, which means the discard logic fired and flattened everything per-facet. On top of that, my snap reporting is generating massive spam with hundreds of duplicate "plane/plane: no junction curve" messages on the per-facet models, which points to a problem with how the adjacency reporting is configured.
> 
> The root cause is that adjacent per-facet planes on a smooth surface are naturally tangent to each other (normals within 2°), so every adjacent pair gets flagged as an unhandled tangent junction. But that's not actually a junction at all — it's just the same surface discretized into facets. A plane/plane tangent pair is either coplanar or two facets of a discretized surface, so there's no real junction to snap. I need to reclassify this as out-of-scope rather than a problem.
> 
> The fix is straightforward: `LocusFailure::PointOrPlanePair` shouldn't count as a problem since plane/plane pairs genuinely have no junction curve (two distinct planes meet in a line; if they're tangent they're coplanar, meaning they're the same surface). So plane/plane tangent equals coplanar equals not a junction. The same logic applies to plane/sphere tangent cases.
> 
> I'm updating `is_problem()` to return false for `NoLocus(PointOrPlanePair)` and documenting it as "no junction curve exists (out of scope)". I want to keep genuinely unhandled cases like `ConePlaneRuling` and `NotCoaxial` flagged as problems, so I'm checking whether the cone and plane are coaxial — if not, that's a real unhandled case that needs attention.
> 
> Actually, I'm realizing there's a bug in my dispatch logic: for a cone tangent to a plane along a ruling, the plane normal should satisfy |n·a| = sin(half_angle), not ≈0. My current check only catches cylinders (where half_angle=0), so cone-plane ruling tangencies are falling through and incorrectly reporting `NotCoaxial`. I need to fix the dispatch to properly test for the ruling-tangency condition so these cases get classified as `ConePlaneRuling` instead.
> 
> I've also spotted two reporting-accuracy issues in what I committed: plane-plane and plane-sphere pairs are being flagged as problems when they should be out of scope, and cone-plane ruling tangencies are misreported as `NotCoaxial`. These don't affect the pipeline behavior since snap doesn't act on any of them, but they're making the diagnostics unreliable on facet-heavy models. Let me fix both of these issues first, then move on to `LEFTOVER_BLOB_MAX`.
> 
> I should also keep an eye on the performance impact of `analyze_pairs` running over thousands of surfaces on these models — with bspline_blister having 2137 surfaces and ~4000 pairs, the `is_tangent_pair` checks and locus building could add up. Let me watch the Stage 2.4 timing to see if there's a bottleneck.

    /// a plane grazes a sphere at a single point rather than along a curve.
    NoJunctionExists,''')
s=s.replace('LocusFailure::PointOrPlanePair => "plane/plane or plane/sphere: no junction curve"','LocusFailure::NoJunctionExists => "plane/plane or plane/sphere: no junction curve exists"')
s=s.replace('Err(LocusFailure::PointOrPlanePair)','Err(LocusFailure::NoJunctionExists)')

s=s.replace('Err(LocusFailure::PointOrPlanePair)','Err(LocusFailure::NoJunctionExists)')

# 2. Only report as a problem the failures that name a junction type we could
#    build and have not.
s=s.replace('''    /// True when snap took responsibility for the pair and something is wrong
    /// — the cases the caller reports loudly.
    pub(crate) fn is_problem(&self) -> bool {
        matches!(
            self.outcome,
            PairOutcome::NoLocus(_) | PairOutcome::Rejected(_)
        )
    }''','''    /// True when snap took responsibility for the pair and something is wrong
    /// — the cases the caller reports loudly.
    ///
    /// A pair whose surfaces simply have no junction between them is not one
    /// of those: it is out of scope in the same way a transversal junction is.
    /// This matters in practice, not just in principle — a smooth surface left
    /// as per-facet planes makes every adjacent facet pair a tangent
    /// plane/plane pair, which would bury a real report under thousands of
    /// lines on exactly the models most likely to have one.
    pub(crate) fn is_problem(&self) -> bool {
        match &self.outcome {
            PairOutcome::NoLocus(LocusFailure::NoJunctionExists) => false,
            PairOutcome::NoLocus(_) | PairOutcome::Rejected(_) => true,
            PairOutcome::Transversal | PairOutcome::Snapped { .. } => false,
        }
    }''')

# 3. A plane grazes a CONE along a ruling when its normal makes the half-angle
#    with the axis, not when it is perpendicular to it. Testing for the
#    cylinder condition alone sent every cone-plane ruling to "not coaxial".
s=s.replace('''    if let Some((plane, cone, flip)) = as_plane_conical(a, b) {
        if dot(plane.normal, cone.axis_direction).abs() < COAXIAL_TOL {
            if !cone.is_cylinder() {
                return Err(LocusFailure::ConePlaneRuling);
            }
            let locus = cylinder_ruling_locus(plane, cone)?;
            return Ok(if flip { locus.flipped() } else { locus });
        }
    }''','''    if let Some((plane, cone, flip)) = as_plane_conical(a, b) {
        // Along a ruling the conical surface's normal equals ±the plane's, and
        // a cone's normal makes the angle (90° − half-angle) with its axis —
        // so the test is |n·a| = sin(half_angle), which is 0 only in the
        // cylinder case. Testing for the cylinder condition alone reported
        // every cone-plane ruling tangency as "not coaxial".
        let axial = dot(plane.normal, cone.axis_direction).abs();
        if (axial - cone.half_angle.sin()).abs() < COAXIAL_TOL {
            if !cone.is_cylinder() {
                return Err(LocusFailure::ConePlaneRuling);
            }
            let locus = cylinder_ruling_locus(plane, cone)?;
            return Ok(if flip { locus.flipped() } else { locus });
        }
    }''')
open(p,'w').write(s)
print('ok')

/// Dissolve into the per-facet residual any committed surface whose boundary
/// with that residual is more fragmented than the surface itself, and return
/// the indices dissolved.
///
/// This replaces the old whole-region discard, which threw away a region's
/// entire decomposition whenever freeform left a connected leftover blob
/// bigger than a fixed size. The premise it protected is real — a surface
/// abutting a jagged per-facet blob reconstructs to an invalid wire — but the
/// remedy was wildly out of proportion to it, and *size was the wrong
/// quantity*. Measured: `cone_tangent_planes` leaves a blob covering 73% of
/// its region and reconstructs with zero BRepCheck failures, while
/// `bspline_blister` leaves one covering 43% and produces sixteen invalid
/// faces — so no threshold on the blob, absolute or relative, separates them.
///
/// What does separate them is *where the invalidity comes from*: a face's wire
/// gains one edge per distinct per-facet neighbour, so the face that goes
/// invalid is the one whose boundary has been shattered into more pieces than
/// the face has substance. Comparing a surface's per-facet neighbour count
/// against its own face count says exactly that, carries no length and no
/// tuned number, and dissolves only the surfaces that are actually in trouble
/// rather than every surface that happens to share a region with them.
///
/// Iterated to a fixpoint, because dissolving one surface enlarges the
/// residual and can shatter its neighbour's boundary in turn. In the limit
/// this reproduces the old whole-region behaviour — but only when every
/// surface in the region individually earns it.
fn dissolve_fragmented_surfaces(
    mesh: &ConnectedMesh,
    hyps: &[CompeteHyp],
    already_dissolved: &HashSet<usize>,
    residual: &mut Vec<usize>,
) -> HashSet<usize> {
    let mut dissolved: HashSet<usize> = HashSet::new();
    let mut in_residual: HashSet<usize> = residual.iter().copied().collect();
    loop {
        let mut round: Vec<usize> = Vec::new();
        for (i, hyp) in hyps.iter().enumerate() {
            if already_dissolved.contains(&i) || dissolved.contains(&i) {
                continue;
            }
            let own: HashSet<usize> = hyp.faces().iter().copied().collect();
            let mut neighbours: HashSet<usize> = HashSet::new();
            for &fi in hyp.faces() {
                let vc = mesh.faces[fi].vertex_count as usize;
                for &ni in &mesh.faces[fi].neighbors[..vc] {
                    if ni >= 0 {
                        let ni = ni as usize;
                        if in_residual.contains(&ni) && !own.contains(&ni) {
                            neighbours.insert(ni);
                        }
                    }
                }
            }
            if neighbours.len() > hyp.faces().len() {
                round.push(i);
            }
        }
        if round.is_empty() {
            return dissolved;
        }
        for i in round {
            dissolved.insert(i);
            for &fi in hyps[i].faces() {
                if in_residual.insert(fi) {
                    residual.push(fi);
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

> Now I'm seeing the real issue — the remaining failures are single-mesh-face per-facet planes where each face is just a triangle or quad with 3 or 4 edges. These aren't invalid because of the geometry itself, but because their edges are degenerate or micro-slivers, especially where they meet analytic surfaces or neighboring facets. This is the same micro-sliver problem from the 3DBenchy work, not the case where analytic surfaces get isolated in a blob. The key insight is that my approach needs to handle these edge degeneracies differently.
> 
> The old guard's solution was to per-facet the entire region, which fundamentally changed the edge structure and happened to sidestep these problems — but that's incidental, not a real fix for the stated mechanism. So I need to decide whether the trade-off is worth it: with my change, cone_tangent_planes unblocks a test and works cleanly, but blister goes from a valid but empty polyhedron with 2137 per-facet planes to a mostly-decomposed model with 968 surfaces (9 analytic) and 4 invalid slivers, while saddle improves slightly. The old behavior is "valid" but potentially hollow, whereas the new approach gives more geometric content at the cost of these edge failures.
> 
> I could track blister as a known-invalid case with test coverage, try to dissolve the slivers' problematic neighbors directly, or accept that I can't diagnose this deeper without more time. But stepping back — the user asked me to fix the LEFTOVER_BLOB_MAX cliff by making it proportionate. I've diagnosed that absolute or relative size can't separate these cases, replaced it with a local, boundary-fragmentation-keyed rule, and the result unblocks a test while keeping everything else stable and reducing blister's invalid faces from 16 down to 4.
> 
> The trade-off is that blister and saddle regressed from fully valid under the old guard. The real issue is that blister's 926-face blob has a freeform fit that fails the pole-bound check — the guard is correctly rejecting a bad fit, but then nothing else can handle it.
> 
> My approach is to keep the local rule but add a region-level safety net: if the residual still dominates after dissolution, fall back to per-faceting the whole region. The problem is that a relative gate doesn't cleanly separate cone_tangent_planes from blister, and I need to remeasure how the numbers shift after the dissolution rule actually runs.
> 
> Rather than inventing a threshold to hide the issue, I should measure the full suite and make an honest call: keep the local rule structure, document the blister/saddle regression, and give those models proper test coverage so the behavior is visible and pinned rather than silently regressing.
> 
> The real problem is that I'd be shipping a solid that now fails BRepCheck validation when it previously passed — that's a regression on an untested model, and the project standard is to flag it, not hide it. Let me reconsider the old condition once more to see if there's a better path forward. I'm testing whether a region-level threshold could separate these cases, but the numbers aren't cooperating. For cone_tangent_planes, the surviving surfaces cover far less area than the residual, which would trigger the rule and discard the cones—exactly wrong. This suggests no region-level statistic can distinguish between a genuinely failed decomposition and one that's just sparse but valid.
> 
> So I'm accepting that the local rule is the right answer, and the blister/saddle invalidity is a separate issue to address independently. I'll run the test suite now, add coverage for these edge cases, document the findings, and commit.

/// Minimum number of mesh faces for a B-spline fit attempt. A bicubic patch
/// has many DOF; below this the region is noise (and DEVELOPMENT_PLAN §2.7
/// specifies ≥ 4).
pub(crate) const MIN_BSPLINE_FACES: usize = 4;

/// Selections up to this many faces are candidates for absorption into a
/// freeform region they connect to smoothly. Freeform surfaces bait the
/// analytic detectors locally: an inflection produces short runs of
/// accidentally-coplanar facets fitted as tiny planes (bspline_wave),
/// bands of near-constant curvature fit as narrow cylinder ribbons
/// (bspline_saddle: 16 six-face cylinders carving the patch apart), and a
/// Gaussian bump peak fits 9–12-face cones (hill_with_hole). Left
/// selected, they punch holes in the freeform region and leave fake
/// feature edges. Real small features are protected twice: a component
/// with no single-face planar member is never fitted, and absorbed
/// non-single faces must not outnumber the single-face leftovers (see
/// \`deduce_bspline_surfaces\`).

// neighbours from absorption too. Fit quality replaces it — see

/// Precision passed to ShapeAnalysis_Surface projections (mm). This is the

I've stopped short of a fix, because I hit a design question rather than a bug. The tree is back at the committed state — suite 511 passing / 3 ignored, probe identical. Findings recorded in `b0db5ca`.

## What I found

**The NURBS corpus is 5 of 8 healthy.** `bspline_hill`, `bspline_terrain`, `bspline_wave`, `elliptical_arch`, `elliptical_cylinder` all pass full `--compare` at 0.000000e0 mm. Freeform fitting itself is in good shape.

The three failures are **two different bugs**:

**`hill_with_hole`** — competition carves the freeform hill into 40 spurious analytic patches (47 surfaces against a reference 7). All 7 correct surfaces are present, including the hole cylinder at r=5.0000 fitted to 1.8e-6; the 40 extras are 4–23-face cones and spheres covering 2–8 mm² of a 1541 mm² hill.

**`bspline_blister` / `bspline_saddle`** — the freeform fit itself is rejected by the §2.7 pole-bound check (blister's 926-face component reports control points 2749.5 mm outside the data bounding box), so nothing explains those components at all.

## Why I stopped

The mechanism that should catch hill_with_hole's litter is the stage-2.3(e) island absorption, whose candidacy rule is too weak two ways: the accidents run to 23 faces past a 16-face cap, and because the same test decides which surfaces count as "real" for enclosure, the accidents just over the cap mark *themselves* real and disqualify their smaller neighbours too.

I tried four replacements and measured three of them wrong:

- **Fit quality** — very tempting, since the accidents sit 200–800× worse than the genuine surfaces with `--vertex-tolerance` sitting in the gap. Wrong in general: **an accidental fit is frequently an excellent fit** — a run of coplanar facets along an inflection really is planar. `bspline_hill`: 6 surfaces → 2719.
- **A fraction of the region** — fixed both hills, broke the elliptical models (a fraction is stricter than a count on small regions).
- **Smaller than the region's total leftovers** — fixed hill_with_hole to exactly 7 surfaces and kept the ellipticals, but broke stepped_block medium 81 → 84 (scattered slivers along seams aren't a patch).
- **Smaller than the largest connected leftover patch** — probe clean, every NURBS model at its best, but it dissolves `cone_tangent_planes`' real cones and re-breaks the test I'd just re-enabled.

The reason none works: **a B-spline can fit anything, a cone included**, so "the freeform patch validates over these faces" is not evidence the region is freeform. The window the corpus actually demands is 13.5%–18.6% of the patch — that's overfitting, not a criterion. This needs real model selection between a B-spline and an analytic surface on the same support. Worth noting that item 2's complexity-pricing refutation doesn't obviously transfer: that was about *nested analytic* types differing by 1–2 DOF, whereas here it's a B-spline's dozens against a cone's six.

## Two things worth knowing regardless

**`cone_tangent_planes` has been passing for an accidental reason.** Its region's freeform fit fails as ill-conditioned, and that is the only thing leaving its cones alone. Give the freeform rung a better-conditioned domain and it swallows a real cone. Treat that test as fragile.

**Fixing candidacy wouldn't be sufficient for hill_with_hole anyway.** With the decomposition corrected to exactly 7 surfaces it clears stage 3.1 and then fails stage 4.1 on volume at 6.96e-2 — a second, downstream problem.

## What I'd do next

Start with **blister/saddle**, not hill_with_hole: it's a fitting problem with a clear diagnostic signal (the pole-bound rejection), rather than a model-selection argument that needs designing. And I'd add `--compare` coverage across the whole NURBS corpus first — five of eight models being unwatched is how all of this stayed invisible, and the reference STEPs are already sitting there.

fn residual_scale<S: SurfaceType>(mesh: &ConnectedMesh, faces: &[usize], fit: &S::Fit) -> f64 {
    let verts = vertices_of(mesh, faces);
    if verts.is_empty() {
        return 0.0;
    }
    let mut d: Vec<f64> = verts
        .iter()
        .map(|&vi| {
            let v = &mesh.vertices[vi];
            S::vertex_distance(fit, &[v.x, v.y, v.z])
        })
        .collect();
    d.sort_by(|a, b| a.partial_cmp(b).unwrap_or(std::cmp::Ordering::Equal));
    d[d.len() / 2]
}

/// The tolerance at which a fit may claim a face: what the fit's own accuracy
/// justifies, bounded below by the user's stated precision and above by
/// \`GROW_VTOL_FACTOR\`.
///
/// A mesh vertex lies on the true CAD surface to ~1e-6 mm — measured across the
/// corpus, and on coarse tessellations too (rounded_cube fine 1.9e-6,
/// stepped_block fine 1.2e-5). So a face that really belongs to a surface
/// misses its fit by the *fit's* error and nothing else, while a face that does
/// not belong misses it by a geometric departure: one tessellation row past a
/// tangent junction sits ~h²/2r away. Those are different quantities, and the
/// gap between them is enormous — the row that used to be swallowed on

///
/// A single absolute bar cannot see that, because it has to be loose enough for
/// the worst-conditioned fit in the corpus and is then hundreds of times too
/// loose for a converged one. Scaling by the fit's own residuals is
/// self-calibrating: a fit still being bootstrapped off a partial patch reports
/// a large scale and keeps the room it needs to grow, and the bar tightens on
/// its own as the support fills in and the fit converges.
///
/// The bounds are not tuning. The floor is \`--vertex-tolerance\`, the precision
/// the user asked for, below which no distinction is claimed. The ceiling is
/// the old fixed bar, so this can only ever be *tighter* than the previous
/// behaviour, never looser — today's bar is simply pinned at that ceiling.
fn acceptance_tol<S: SurfaceType>(
    mesh: &ConnectedMesh,
    faces: &[usize],
    fit: &S::Fit,
    config: &Config,
) -> f64 {
    let floor = config.vertex_tolerance_mm;
    let ceiling = floor * GROW_VTOL_FACTOR;
    (RESIDUAL_SIGMAS * residual_scale::<S>(mesh, faces, fit)).clamp(floor, ceiling)
}

> I'm identifying the three core design decisions behind this algorithm: why it uses self-calibration instead of fixed tolerances, why it establishes a lower bound at the vertex tolerance, and why it caps the adjustment at 30 times that baseline value.
> 
> The fundamental insight is that mesh vertices sit on the true CAD surface to within about 1 micrometer, but the facet interiors sag away. When a face genuinely belongs to a surface, it misses the fit by only the fit's own error—a tiny amount. When a face doesn't belong, it misses by a geometric departure that's orders of magnitude larger. A single fixed tolerance can't distinguish between these two cases because the fit's error itself varies wildly throughout the algorithm's execution and across different models.
> 
> Scaling the acceptance threshold by the fit's own residuals solves this elegantly: the criterion stays loose while the fit is still bootstrapping from a small seed patch (where residuals are around 0.1 micrometers), then automatically tightens as the support converges (where residuals drop to 1 micrometer). The proof is in the results—using a scaled threshold at 5, 8, or 15 sigma produces identical decompositions across that entire range, whereas the old absolute bar collapsed completely over a much smaller variation. Using the median instead of RMS also matters because the leaked faces are actually present in the sample, so the median stays tight at the true scale while the RMS gets inflated by outliers.
> 
> The floor is set at the user's stated `--vertex-tolerance` because that's the only genuine precision request in the system—everything else is either derived from exporter settings or self-calibrated. Below that threshold, the pipeline doesn't claim to distinguish anything, so no matter how good the fit becomes, the bar never tightens past what the user explicitly asked for. Without this floor, a perfectly converged fit with a 1e-9 residual would demand impossibly tight tolerances and reject legitimate faces.
> 
> The ceiling at 30× is where things get tricky. Every self-calibrating criterion has the same failure mode: a poor fit produces a large residual scale, which admits more foreign faces, which makes the fit worse, which inflates the scale further—a positive feedback loop that can spiral out of control.
> 
> The ceiling acts as a brake on that spiral. It's load-bearing and measured; removing it causes real degradation in the results—bspline_wave loses its single freeform patch and stepped_block fine loses its exact decomposition. I chose 30× specifically because it was the old fixed bar, so this change could only ever tighten the criterion relative to previous behavior, never loosen it—a deliberately conservative migration. The value itself was sized around what a bootstrapping fit needs: roughly 1e-4 mm residual from partial support, which sits well above the default vertex tolerance but far below the divergence you'd see on a coarse mesh past a tangent junction.
> 
> What actually happened here—and the project's own notes make this clear—is that `GROW_VTOL_FACTOR` got demoted from the operative value to a safety ceiling, while `RESIDUAL_SIGMAS` was introduced as the new operative bar. It's three separate decisions stacked together, and they have different justifications. The code is [compete.rs:674](src/stage2/compete.rs:674).

## Why self-calibrate at all

The flood has to answer "does this face belong to this surface?", and the whole design rests on one measured fact: **a mesh vertex lies on the true CAD surface to ~1e-6 mm** — rounded_cube fine 1.9e-6, stepped_block fine 1.2e-5, and coarse tessellations too (part_rounded_cube coarse 2.98e-6). Tessellators put vertices *on* the surface; it's the facet interiors that sag.

That splits the question into two quantities that aren't comparable:

- A face that **belongs** misses its fit by the **fit's own error**, and nothing else.
- A face that **doesn't belong** misses it by a **geometric departure** — one tessellation row past a tangent junction sits ~h²/2r away.

The gap is enormous. The row that used to get swallowed on stepped_block fine was 9.5e-4 mm from a fit accurate to 1e-6 — about **950× the fit's own scale**, where a genuine face sits at ~1×.

No single absolute bar can straddle that, because the fit's own error moves by orders of magnitude *during the algorithm*: bootstrapping off a small seed patch it's ~1e-4 mm; converged on full support it's ~1e-6. A fixed bar has to be loose enough for the worst bootstrap, and is then ~100× too loose for a converged fit — which is precisely how junction rows leak. Scaling by the fit's own residuals gives the bar room while the fit is still finding itself and tightens it automatically as the support fills in.

The payoff is insensitivity, not the value: **identical corpus decompositions at 5, 8 and 15 sigmas**, where the absolute bar it replaced went from correct to total collapse over a 3.3× change.

One detail that matters — [residual_scale](src/stage2/compete.rs:633) takes the **median**, not RMS, because the faces the criterion exists to detect are sitting *in the sample*. 85 good faces plus 10 leaked at 9.5e-4 give an RMS of 3.1e-4, still loose enough to admit them; the median stays at 1e-6.

## Why the floor at `--vertex-tolerance`

That's the user's stated precision, and it's the one tolerance in the system that's a genuine user request rather than a stand-in for a setting the exporter discarded (`--surface-tolerance` and `--angular-tolerance` are the stand-ins — that's TODO item B). Below it the pipeline doesn't claim to distinguish anything. Without the floor, a converged fit reporting 1e-9 would demand 5e-9 of its faces and start rejecting legitimate ones.

## Why the ceiling at 30×

This is the honest weak point, and it's there for the reason **every** self-calibrating criterion needs a brake: it's a positive feedback loop. A poor fit reports a large residual scale → admits more foreign faces → fits worse → inflates the scale further. The ceiling stops the runaway.

It's load-bearing and measured: remove it and `bspline_wave` loses its single freeform patch (6 surfaces → 16) and stepped_block fine loses its exact decomposition (71 → 74).

The specific value of 30 is not independently derived — it is **the old fixed bar, unchanged**. That was deliberate: keeping it as the ceiling means the new criterion can only ever be *tighter* than the previous behaviour, never looser, so the migration couldn't regress anything by loosening. Its original sizing was "what a bootstrapping fit needs": ~1e-4 mm residual from partial support, comfortably above the 5e-5 default vertex tolerance, yet far below the ~0.1 mm a neighbouring surface diverges by one row past a tangent junction on a coarse mesh.

## The part worth being blunt about

This change **did not remove a constant**, and the project's own notes say so. `GROW_VTOL_FACTOR` was demoted from the operative value to a safety ceiling, and `RESIDUAL_SIGMAS` was added in its place — 35 constants before, 35 after. What improved is that the *operative* bar became scale-free: it carries no length, so it needs no recalibration per model, per feature size, or per tessellation density. The remaining absolute numbers are a floor the user sets and a ceiling that only ever restricts.

That's also why it's on the ablation list in TODO: both `GROW_VTOL_FACTOR` and `RESIDUAL_SIGMAS` belong to the flood, which item C (variational shape approximation) would replace outright.
